name: Abdominal pain
description: Abdominal pain is pain felt anywhere between the chest and the groin, arising from abdominal organs, the abdominal wall or referred from outside the abdomen. Its location, character, timing and associated features guide the differential, and severity does not always reflect seriousness.
weight_rationale: Abdominal pain without localisation is common to many gastrointestinal, urinary, gynecological and systemic conditions.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia

name: Abdominal swelling (distension or ascites)
description: Abdominal swelling is enlargement of the abdomen from gas, fluid, organ enlargement or masses. Ascites, free fluid in the peritoneal cavity, most often results from portal hypertension and low serum albumin in chronic liver disease, including the periportal fibrosis of chronic Schistosoma japonicum infection, and is suggested by shifting dullness and a fluid wave.
weight_rationale: Distension alone is nonspecific (gas, obesity, pregnancy); demonstrable ascites narrows the differential to cirrhosis and portal hypertension, heart failure, malignancy and hypoalbuminemic states.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia; StatPearls

name: Acid regurgitation (sour fluid or food coming back up)
description: Effortless backflow of sour or bitter stomach contents into the throat or mouth, without the retching of vomiting. It is, with heartburn, one of the two typical symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux disease and is often worse after large meals, when bending over or when lying down.
weight_rationale: Heartburn and regurgitation are the two typical symptoms of GERD; together, without alarm features, they support a presumptive diagnosis.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; StatPearls - Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease

name: Agitation, anxiety or hallucinations
description: Agitation is a state of excessive motor and mental restlessness with irritability or anxiety, which may be accompanied by hallucinations when perception is disturbed. It arises from psychiatric illness but also from delirium due to infection, metabolic disturbance, intoxication or withdrawal, and is a feature of furious rabies.
weight_rationale: Agitation is nonspecific, but new agitation or hallucinations with fever suggest delirium or encephalitis (including rabies) and mandate urgent evaluation.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia; World Health Organization

name: Black, tarry stools (melena)
description: Melena is the passage of black, sticky, tarry stools with a characteristic foul odour, produced when blood from the upper gastrointestinal tract is digested. It usually indicates bleeding from the esophagus, stomach or duodenum; iron and bismuth can blacken stools but do not make them tarry.
weight_rationale: Tarry black stool localises bleeding to the upper gastrointestinal tract, most commonly peptic ulcer disease.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf); MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia

name: Blister-like rash (vesicles)
description: A vesicular rash consists of small (under about 1 cm), fluid-filled elevations of the skin. In varicella the vesicles appear in successive crops, starting on the face and trunk, so lesions at all stages from macules to crusts coexist; other patterns include grouped vesicles (herpes simplex), dermatomal vesicles (zoster) and hand-foot-mouth distributions (enterovirus).
weight_rationale: Vesicles narrow the differential to a limited group of viral, contact and bullous conditions, and the pattern (crops at different stages, dermatomal, hand-foot-mouth) often points to a specific diagnosis.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia; StatPearls

name: Blood in stool (hematochezia)
description: Hematochezia is the passage of bright red or maroon blood per rectum, alone or mixed with stool. It usually indicates a colonic, rectal or anal source, although brisk upper gastrointestinal bleeding can also present this way; bloody diarrhea with fever suggests invasive infectious or inflammatory colitis.
weight_rationale: Visible blood localizes the problem to the gastrointestinal tract, most often the lower tract, but the range of causes remains wide from hemorrhoids to colitis, schistosomiasis and colorectal cancer.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia; StatPearls

name: Blood in urine (hematuria / cola-colored urine)
description: Red, pink or brown (cola- or tea-colored) urine caused by red blood cells, or blood found only on urine testing. Brown urine with red cell casts suggests bleeding from the glomeruli (glomerulonephritis); bright red urine with clots more often comes from the bladder or urinary tract.
weight_rationale: Visible blood or cola-colored urine with swelling and high blood pressure points to glomerulonephritis; isolated hematuria has many other causes.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; StatPearls - Poststreptococcal Glomerulonephritis

name: Blurred vision
description: Blurred vision is loss of sharpness of vision and inability to see fine details. It may result from refractive errors, lens changes from high blood glucose, cataract, retinal or optic nerve disease, and neurological causes.
weight_rationale: Blurred vision is shared by ocular, metabolic and neurological disorders and discriminates moderately.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia

name: Breathlessness lying flat (orthopnea)
description: Orthopnea is breathlessness in the recumbent position that is relieved by sitting or standing, often quantified by the number of pillows needed to sleep. It is characteristic of left ventricular failure due to redistribution of fluid into the pulmonary circulation, and often occurs with paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.
weight_rationale: Orthopnea is a relatively specific symptom of heart failure with raised pulmonary venous pressure.

name: Bulging or staring eyes (proptosis)
description: Forward displacement of one or both eyeballs, often with eyelid retraction, a staring look, gritty or watery eyes and sometimes double vision. Graves orbitopathy is the most common cause in adults; one-sided or rapidly progressive proptosis needs urgent assessment for orbital infection or tumor.
weight_rationale: Bulging eyes with lid retraction in a person with hyperthyroidism is highly specific for Graves disease (Graves orbitopathy).

name: Calf muscle pain / tenderness
description: Calf pain is pain or tenderness localized to the posterior lower leg muscles. In an acute febrile illness, myalgia characteristically involving the calves and lower back is a recognized feature of leptospirosis; outside that context, calf pain is often musculoskeletal or vascular.
weight_rationale: Febrile illness with prominent calf muscle pain is a classic pointer toward leptospirosis, especially after flood or animal-urine exposure.

name: Chalky lumps under the skin near joints or ears (tophi)
description: Firm, painless, whitish or yellowish lumps formed by deposits of urate crystals, typically over the toes, fingers, elbows, Achilles tendon or ear rims. They appear after years of high uric acid and can discharge chalky material or damage joints.
weight_rationale: Tophi indicate long-standing, poorly controlled gout and are an indication for urate-lowering therapy.

name: Chest pain or pressure (angina-like)
description: Anginal chest pain is typically a dull, heavy, pressing or crushing substernal discomfort that may radiate to the arm, neck or jaw, is precipitated by exertion or stress and relieved by rest. Chest pain has a broad differential that includes several immediately life-threatening causes.
weight_rationale: Pressure-like substernal pain with exertional features points toward myocardial ischemia, though other thoracic causes overlap.

name: Chest tightness
description: Chest tightness is a sensation of constriction or inability to fully expand the chest. It is one of the cardinal symptoms of asthma, often reported more frequently than wheeze, but a sensation of tightness or pressure may also represent myocardial ischemia.
weight_rationale: Chest tightness with wheeze or cough favours bronchospasm, although overlap with cardiac ischemic pain limits specificity.

name: Chills / rigors
description: Chills are a sensation of coldness, often with shivering and pallor, that occur as body temperature rises toward a newly elevated set point. Rigors are intense, uncontrollable shaking chills ('teeth-chattering, bed-shaking') that are associated with rapid temperature rise and suggest bacteremia or other acute infection.
weight_rationale: Chills accompany most febrile illnesses, although true rigors modestly favour bacteremia, malaria, pyelonephritis and similar infections.

name: Confusion / altered mental status
description: Confusion is the inability to think as clearly or quickly as usual, with disorientation and difficulty with attention, memory and decisions. Acute confusion (delirium) is a medical emergency commonly caused by infection, metabolic derangement, hypoxia, drugs or brain disease.
weight_rationale: Acute confusion signals serious illness but arises from many systemic and neurological causes.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia

name: Constipation
description: Constipation is infrequent bowel movements (commonly fewer than three per week) or hard, dry stools that are difficult or painful to pass. It is most often functional or dietary, but may reflect medicines, metabolic disease or bowel obstruction.
weight_rationale: Constipation is common and usually functional, adding limited diagnostic information on its own.

name: Cough
description: Cough is a protective reflex that expels air forcefully to clear the airways of secretions and irritants. It is classified as acute (under 3 weeks), subacute (3-8 weeks) or chronic (over 8 weeks) and may be dry or productive.
weight_rationale: Cough is common to most respiratory infections and many airway diseases and discriminates poorly alone.

name: Coughing fits with a "whoop" (paroxysmal cough)
description: Paroxysmal cough consists of bursts of rapid, uncontrollable coughs on a single expiration, followed by a forced inspiration against a partially closed glottis that produces the characteristic high-pitched whoop. It is the defining feature of the paroxysmal stage of pertussis, although the whoop is often absent in young infants and in adolescents and adults.
weight_rationale: Paroxysms with an inspiratory whoop are highly characteristic of pertussis and strongly narrow the differential, though absence of the whoop does not exclude it.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; StatPearls; MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia

name: Coughing up blood (hemoptysis)
description: Hemoptysis is the expectoration of blood or blood-tinged sputum originating from the lungs or tracheobronchial tree, distinguished from bleeding from the nose, mouth or upper gastrointestinal tract. Massive hemoptysis is a life-threatening emergency.
weight_rationale: Coughing up blood narrows the differential to a limited set of pulmonary causes, prominently tuberculosis, bronchitis, bronchiectasis, lung cancer and pulmonary embolism.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; Clinical Methods (NCBI Bookshelf); MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia

name: Craving ice, soil or other non-food items (pica)
description: Persistent craving for and eating of non-food substances such as ice (pagophagia), clay or soil (geophagia), starch or chalk. Pica is a recognised feature of iron deficiency, with or without anemia, and is also seen in pregnancy, young children and some developmental conditions.
weight_rationale: Pica, especially pagophagia (craving ice), is a fairly specific clue to iron deficiency and often improves quickly with iron replacement.

causes: ["Iron deficiency","Pregnancy","Developmental disorders and autism spectrum disorder","Zinc deficiency","Cultural practices"]

name: Dark urine
description: Dark urine is urine that is dark yellow, tea- or cola-coloured. Dark brown clear urine may reflect bilirubinuria from liver disease, while dark urine can also result from severe dehydration, rhabdomyolysis, hemoglobinuria, blood in the urine or certain foods and medicines.
weight_rationale: Tea- or cola-coloured urine narrows the differential to liver disease, hemolysis, rhabdomyolysis or hematuria.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia

name: Decreased urine output (oliguria)
description: Oliguria is reduced urine output, commonly defined in adults as less than 400 mL per day (or below about 0.5 mL/kg/h). Causes are classified as prerenal (reduced kidney perfusion, e.g., dehydration or shock), intrinsic renal and postrenal (urinary obstruction).
weight_rationale: Reduced urine output points to hypovolemia, shock or acute kidney injury rather than to a specific disease.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia; StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf)
causes: ["Dehydration (vomiting, diarrhea, poor intake)","Shock or sepsis","Acute kidney injury (e.g., leptospirosis, severe malaria)","Heart failure","Urinary tract obstruction","Nephrotoxic medicines"]

name: Diarrhea
description: Diarrhea is the passage of loose or watery stools, typically three or more times a day. Acute diarrhea is most often infectious, while chronic diarrhea suggests malabsorptive, inflammatory or functional disease.
weight_rationale: Diarrhea points toward intestinal involvement, most often acute infectious gastroenteritis, but also occurs in systemic infections.

name: Difficulty swallowing (dysphagia)
description: A sensation that food or liquid sticks or passes slowly on the way from the mouth to the stomach. Oropharyngeal dysphagia (trouble starting a swallow, coughing or choking) usually has a neurologic or muscular cause, while esophageal dysphagia (food sticking behind the breastbone) suggests a stricture, ring, motility disorder or tumor. In GERD it is an alarm feature.
weight_rationale: Dysphagia is not specific to one disease, but it is an alarm feature: in reflux it suggests stricture or malignancy and calls for endoscopy.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; StatPearls - Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease

name: Dizziness / lightheadedness
description: Dizziness is a term used for two main symptoms: lightheadedness (a feeling of faintness) and vertigo (a false sense of spinning or movement). Lightheadedness often reflects reduced blood flow to the brain, while vertigo usually reflects inner ear or brainstem disease.
weight_rationale: Dizziness is common and arises from cardiovascular, vestibular, metabolic, medication and neurological causes.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia

name: Epigastric pain
description: Epigastric pain is pain or burning located in the upper central abdomen below the xiphoid process. It is characteristic of peptic ulcer disease, gastritis and functional dyspepsia, but cardiac, biliary and pancreatic disease may also present here.
weight_rationale: Pain localised to the epigastrium focuses the differential on upper gastrointestinal causes, while still overlapping with cardiac and pancreaticobiliary disease.

name: Excessive salivation / drooling
description: Hypersalivation and drooling result from excess saliva production or, more often, from an inability to retain or swallow normal saliva. Causes range from oral and pharyngeal infections to neurologic disorders that impair swallowing, and in rabies drooling reflects both autonomic stimulation and painful pharyngeal spasms.
weight_rationale: Drooling has a broad differential (oral infection, neuromuscular disease, medications); it gains weight when combined with hydrophobia and agitation after an animal bite, as in rabies.

name: Excessive thirst (polydipsia)
description: Polydipsia is an abnormal, persistent feeling of needing to drink fluids. It usually accompanies polyuria and dehydration, and is a classic symptom of uncontrolled diabetes mellitus.
weight_rationale: Excessive thirst with polyuria is a classic pointer to hyperglycemia and other water-balance disorders.

name: Excessive urination (polyuria)
description: Polyuria is production of abnormally large volumes of urine, generally more than 2.5 L per day in adults, distinct from frequent passage of small volumes. It results from osmotic diuresis (e.g., hyperglycemia), excess fluid intake, diuretics or impaired urine concentration.
weight_rationale: True polyuria, especially with thirst, points to hyperglycemia or other disorders of water balance.

name: Facial droop
description: Facial droop is weakness of the facial muscles causing asymmetry of the face, such as a drooping mouth corner. Stroke typically causes lower facial weakness with forehead sparing, whereas Bell's palsy affects the whole side of the face including the forehead.
weight_rationale: Sudden facial droop is a highly localising neurological sign and a core feature of stroke recognition tools.

name: Fatigue & malaise
description: Fatigue is a feeling of weariness, tiredness or lack of energy that is not relieved by usual rest, and malaise is a general sense of being unwell. Both accompany a very broad range of infectious, metabolic, hematologic, psychiatric and lifestyle-related conditions.
weight_rationale: Fatigue and malaise are among the least specific symptoms and occur in most acute and chronic illnesses.

name: Fear of water / throat spasms on swallowing (hydrophobia)
description: Hydrophobia is a terrifying, involuntary spasm of the pharyngeal, laryngeal and inspiratory muscles provoked by attempts to drink, and in time by the sight, sound or even thought of water. It is the hallmark of furious (encephalitic) rabies and is often accompanied by aerophobia, spasms triggered by a draft of air on the face.
weight_rationale: Hydrophobia is essentially pathognomonic of rabies encephalitis, especially with a history of animal bite, and signals a disease that is fatal once symptomatic.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; StatPearls; MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia

name: Fever
description: Fever is a regulated elevation of body temperature above the individual's normal range, produced when pyrogens reset the hypothalamic thermoregulatory set point. It is most often a response to infection but also accompanies inflammatory, malignant, drug-related and other conditions.
weight_rationale: Fever accompanies a very wide range of infectious and non-infectious illnesses and narrows the differential little on its own.

name: Flank pain
description: Flank pain is pain in one side of the body between the upper abdomen and the back. It commonly arises from the kidney or ureter, as in pyelonephritis or kidney stones, and costovertebral angle tenderness may be present.
weight_rationale: Flank pain localises the process to the kidney or ureter, especially with urinary symptoms or fever.

name: Foamy or bubbly urine
description: Urine that repeatedly forms a frothy layer that does not settle. Occasional foam is normal (forceful stream, concentrated urine), but persistent foaminess can reflect large amounts of protein in the urine (proteinuria), a marker of glomerular kidney damage in diabetes, hypertension and glomerulonephritis.
weight_rationale: Persistently foamy urine can indicate significant proteinuria, an important marker of kidney damage, but it needs urine testing to confirm.

name: Headache
description: Headache is pain in any region of the head, arising from pain-sensitive intracranial or extracranial structures. Most headaches are primary (migraine, tension-type, cluster), but headache also accompanies systemic infection and can signal serious intracranial disease.
weight_rationale: Headache is extremely common and accompanies many primary headache disorders and systemic illnesses, so it has low specificity alone.

name: Heartburn
description: Heartburn is a painful burning feeling just below or behind the breastbone, usually caused by reflux of gastric acid into the esophagus. It is often worse after meals, when lying down or bending over.
weight_rationale: Retrosternal burning related to meals and posture is fairly characteristic of acid reflux and peptic disease.

name: Heat intolerance and excessive sweating
description: Feeling unusually hot, sweaty or uncomfortable in warm surroundings that others tolerate. It reflects increased heat production from a raised metabolic rate and is a classic symptom of hyperthyroidism, together with weight loss, tremor and palpitations.
weight_rationale: Feeling hot and sweaty when others are comfortable, with weight loss and palpitations, is a characteristic pattern of hyperthyroidism.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; StatPearls - Graves Disease

name: Involuntary jerky movements (chorea)
description: Brief, irregular, purposeless movements that flow from one body part to another, often with clumsiness, facial grimacing and emotional lability. In children and adolescents the most common acquired cause is Sydenham chorea, a late manifestation of acute rheumatic fever that can appear months after the streptococcal infection.
weight_rationale: In a child or adolescent, new chorea is a major Jones criterion and is strongly suggestive of acute rheumatic fever (Sydenham chorea), even without other features.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; AHA Scientific Statement - Revision of the Jones Criteria (2015); WHO Fact Sheet - Rheumatic heart disease

name: Itching (pruritus)
description: Pruritus is an unpleasant skin sensation that provokes the desire to scratch. It may be localized, usually from primary skin disease, or generalized, when systemic causes such as cholestatic liver disease, chronic kidney disease, drug reactions or hematologic disorders are considered.
weight_rationale: Itching is very common and nonspecific; it narrows the differential mainly when generalized without rash (suggesting systemic causes such as cholestasis) or when paired with a characteristic eruption such as varicella.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia

name: Jaundice
description: Jaundice is yellow discolouration of the skin, mucous membranes and sclerae caused by accumulation of bilirubin. Scleral icterus is best appreciated when serum bilirubin exceeds about 3 mg/dL, and causes are grouped as prehepatic, hepatic and posthepatic.
weight_rationale: Jaundice localises the problem to hemolysis, liver disease or biliary obstruction, and in febrile illness points toward hepatitis, leptospirosis or severe malaria.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia; StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf)

name: Joint pain (arthralgia)
description: Arthralgia is pain in one or more joints without necessarily visible swelling or inflammation. It may arise from injury, degenerative or inflammatory arthritis, or as part of systemic infection such as dengue ('breakbone fever').
weight_rationale: Joint pain is common in systemic infection and rheumatic disease; its pattern and accompanying features determine how much it narrows the differential.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia; StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf)

name: Joint swelling
description: Joint swelling is enlargement of a joint from synovial fluid (effusion), synovial thickening or swelling of the surrounding soft tissues. It distinguishes true arthritis from arthralgia alone and is characterized by the number and pattern of joints involved, acuity and the presence of warmth or redness.
weight_rationale: Objective swelling separates inflammatory arthritis from simple joint pain and, combined with acuity and joint pattern, narrows the differential to arthritides, crystal disease, septic arthritis and viral arthritis such as chikungunya.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia; World Health Organization

name: Koplik spots
description: Koplik spots are small bluish-white spots, about 2-3 mm, on an erythematous base on the buccal mucosa opposite the molars, likened to 'grains of salt on a red background'. They typically appear about a day before the measles rash and fade as the rash develops.
weight_rationale: Koplik spots are considered pathognomonic of measles, so their presence strongly confirms the diagnosis.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf); MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia

name: Leg swelling (edema)
description: Peripheral edema is abnormal buildup of fluid in the tissues of the feet, ankles and legs, typically pitting on pressure. Bilateral edema suggests systemic causes such as heart, kidney or liver disease or medicines, while unilateral swelling suggests local venous or lymphatic causes.
weight_rationale: Leg edema is shared by cardiac, renal, hepatic, venous and drug-related causes, though distribution helps narrow it.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia

name: Loss of appetite
description: Loss of appetite is a reduced desire to eat; the medical term is anorexia (distinct from the eating disorder anorexia nervosa). It accompanies many acute infections as well as chronic, malignant, psychiatric and medicine-related conditions.
weight_rationale: Reduced appetite is a highly nonspecific accompaniment of many acute and chronic illnesses.

name: Loss of smell or taste
description: Anosmia is partial or total loss of the sense of smell, and ageusia or dysgeusia refers to loss or distortion of taste; because flavour depends largely on smell, the two are often reported together. Sudden loss of smell is a recognised feature of viral upper respiratory infections, notably COVID-19.
weight_rationale: New, sudden loss of smell or taste during an acute respiratory illness is relatively characteristic of COVID-19.

name: Mucosal bleeding / petechiae (gum bleeding, nosebleed)
description: Mucocutaneous bleeding includes petechiae (pinpoint red dots from capillary bleeding), bruising, nosebleeds (epistaxis) and gum bleeding. In dengue, minor mucocutaneous bleeding may occur, and mucosal bleeding is listed as a warning sign of severe dengue; it also reflects thrombocytopenia or coagulation disorders.
weight_rationale: In an acute febrile illness, spontaneous mucosal bleeding or petechiae strongly suggests dengue or another cause of thrombocytopenia or coagulopathy.

name: Muscle aches (myalgia)
description: Myalgia is diffuse or localized pain in skeletal muscles, which may also be felt in the associated tendons, ligaments and fascia. Generalized myalgia is a common feature of systemic viral and bacterial infections, while localized myalgia more often reflects overuse or injury.
weight_rationale: Generalized muscle aches accompany many infections and systemic illnesses and are only weakly discriminating.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia

name: Muscle cramps
description: Muscle cramps are sudden, involuntary and painful contractions of a muscle or muscle group, commonly the calves and feet. They occur with overuse and dehydration and with electrolyte disturbances such as hypokalemia, hyponatremia and hypocalcemia, as in the large fluid and electrolyte losses of cholera.
weight_rationale: Cramps are common and mostly benign; they gain significance mainly alongside profuse diarrhea, diuretic use or renal disease, where they suggest electrolyte depletion.

name: Nausea & vomiting
description: Nausea is an unpleasant sensation of the urge to vomit, and vomiting (emesis) is forceful expulsion of gastric contents through the mouth. Both are common and arise from gastrointestinal, central nervous system, metabolic, drug-related and pregnancy-related causes.
weight_rationale: Nausea and vomiting occur in a very wide range of gastrointestinal and systemic conditions and are nonspecific alone.

name: Night sweats
description: Night sweats are episodes of sweating during sleep severe enough to soak nightclothes or bedding, resulting from exaggeration of the normal circadian temperature rhythm. They may accompany any febrile illness and are classically associated with tuberculosis and lymphoma.
weight_rationale: Drenching night sweats, especially with weight loss or chronic cough, direct attention toward tuberculosis, lymphoma and other chronic infections.

name: One-sided weakness or numbness
description: Hemiparesis is weakness of one side of the body, often with numbness (hemisensory loss). Sudden onset is a hallmark of stroke; middle cerebral artery infarction typically causes contralateral weakness and sensory loss affecting the face and arm more than the leg.
weight_rationale: Sudden one-sided weakness or numbness is a focal neurological deficit that strongly localises to the brain and points toward stroke.

name: Pain or tingling at an animal-bite site
description: Pain, itching, tingling or burning at a healed or healing animal-bite or scratch wound can mark the prodrome of rabies as the virus reaches the dorsal root ganglia. It typically appears with nonspecific fever, malaise and headache weeks to months after the exposure and precedes the neurologic phase.
weight_rationale: New paresthesia at a prior animal-bite site in a febrile patient is a classic early clue to rabies, which is nearly always fatal once clinical signs appear.

name: Painful mouth sores or ulcers
description: Mouth sores are painful breaks or vesicles in the oral mucosa that often cause difficulty eating, drinking and swallowing. Most are aphthous, traumatic or viral (herpes simplex, enteroviruses in hand, foot and mouth disease), but persistent ulcers may reflect systemic, autoimmune, immunodeficient or malignant disease.
weight_rationale: Oral ulcers are common and usually benign; they narrow the differential when combined with a pattern such as a hand-foot rash in a child (HFMD) or vesicles elsewhere (varicella).

name: Painful urination (dysuria)
description: Dysuria is pain, burning, stinging or itching of the urethra or urethral meatus during urination. Acute cystitis is the most common cause, but urethritis, sexually transmitted infections, vaginitis and prostatitis also cause it.
weight_rationale: Dysuria localises disease to the lower urinary or genital tract and strongly favours urinary tract infection.

name: Pale or clay-colored stools
description: Pale, clay-colored (acholic) stools result from reduced delivery of bile pigments to the intestine, so that stercobilin no longer gives stool its normal brown color. The finding indicates cholestasis, either intrahepatic (hepatitis, cirrhosis) or extrahepatic (bile duct obstruction), and usually accompanies jaundice and dark urine.
weight_rationale: Acholic stool points specifically to impaired bile flow and narrows the differential to hepatitis and biliary obstruction; with jaundice and dark urine it forms a characteristic cholestatic triad.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia; StatPearls

name: Pale skin, lips or inner eyelids (pallor)
description: Unusual paleness of the skin and mucous membranes, best seen in the inner lower eyelids (conjunctivae), palms, nail beds and lips. It most often reflects a reduced hemoglobin concentration (anemia) but can also occur with shock or reduced skin blood flow.
weight_rationale: Pallor of the conjunctivae, palms and nail beds is a useful bedside sign of anemia, but it does not identify the cause.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; StatPearls - Iron-Deficiency Anemia

name: Palpitations
description: Palpitations are an awareness of the heartbeat as pounding, racing, fluttering or irregular, felt in the chest, throat or neck. They may be benign or reflect arrhythmia, structural heart disease, anemia, thyrotoxicosis or stimulant use.
weight_rationale: Palpitations point to the heart rhythm but have many benign and systemic causes.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia

name: Pink ring-shaped rash on the trunk (erythema marginatum)
description: A faint pink, non-itchy rash of rings or arcs with pale centres and sharp, raised edges, appearing mainly on the trunk and upper limbs and sparing the face. It comes and goes, may be brought out by heat, and is a rare but specific sign of acute rheumatic fever.
weight_rationale: Erythema marginatum is rare but highly specific; it is a major Jones criterion for acute rheumatic fever.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; AHA Scientific Statement - Revision of the Jones Criteria (2015)

name: Pleuritic chest pain
description: Pleuritic chest pain is sharp, localized pain in the chest, neck or shoulder that worsens with breathing, coughing or sneezing. It results from irritation or inflammation of the parietal pleura; pulmonary embolism is the most frequent serious cause.
weight_rationale: Pain that is sharp and worsened by breathing localises the process to the pleura and narrows the differential to pleural, pulmonary and pericardial causes.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf)

name: Productive cough (sputum)
description: A productive cough brings up sputum from the lower respiratory tract. Purulent sputum (yellow, green, opaque) suggests bacterial infection, rust-coloured sputum is associated with pneumococcal pneumonia, and pink frothy sputum suggests pulmonary edema.
weight_rationale: Sputum production points to lower respiratory tract involvement, and its character (purulent, rusty, blood-streaked) adds diagnostic value.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; Clinical Methods (NCBI Bookshelf); MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia

name: Profuse watery ("rice-water") diarrhea
description: Profuse watery diarrhea consists of large-volume, liquid stools; in cholera it is classically pale, flecked with mucus and described as "rice-water". Toxin-mediated intestinal secretion can cause losses of up to about a liter per hour in adults, producing severe dehydration and hypovolemic shock within hours if fluid is not replaced.
weight_rationale: Painless, high-volume rice-water stools are highly characteristic of cholera and, in the right epidemiologic setting, strongly direct the diagnosis and urgent rehydration.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; World Health Organization; StatPearls

name: Puffy eyelids and face (periorbital edema)
description: Swelling around the eyes and face, usually most obvious on waking and improving during the day. In children it is often the first sign of kidney disease such as post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis or nephrotic syndrome; allergy and insect bites cause similar but usually itchy swelling.
weight_rationale: Facial and eyelid puffiness, worst in the morning, is a typical early sign of nephritic and nephrotic syndromes in children.

name: Purple rash that does not fade when pressed (non-blanching rash)
description: Small red-purple spots (petechiae) or larger bruise-like patches (purpura) that stay visible when a clear glass is pressed against them, because blood has leaked into the skin. With fever it can signal meningococcal septicemia, which can progress within hours; it also occurs with low platelets, dengue and vasculitis.
weight_rationale: In a feverish, unwell person a non-blanching rash is a warning sign of meningococcal septicemia and needs immediate treatment.

name: Red eyes (conjunctivitis / conjunctival suffusion)
description: Red eye results from dilated or swollen blood vessels on the surface of the eye. Conjunctivitis involves inflammation with discharge, whereas conjunctival suffusion is redness without purulent discharge that is characteristic of leptospirosis; conjunctivitis is also part of the measles prodrome.
weight_rationale: In a febrile patient, conjunctival suffusion or conjunctivitis points toward leptospirosis or measles.

name: Retro-orbital pain (pain behind the eyes)
description: Retro-orbital pain is aching or pressure felt behind the eyeball, often worsened by eye movement. In febrile illness it is a characteristic feature of dengue, accompanying severe headache, myalgia and arthralgia; it also occurs with migraine, sinusitis and orbital disease.
weight_rationale: In a febrile patient, pain behind the eyes points fairly strongly toward dengue and other arboviral infections.

name: Right lower abdominal pain (right lower quadrant)
description: Pain felt in the right lower part of the abdomen, below the navel and toward the hip bone. In acute appendicitis it typically begins as vague pain around the navel and moves to the right lower quadrant (McBurney point) over 12-24 hours as the inflamed appendix irritates the overlying peritoneum. Ovarian, tubal, urinary tract and bowel conditions can cause pain in the same area.
weight_rationale: Pain that starts around the navel and settles in the right lower abdomen is the classic pattern of acute appendicitis and points strongly toward it, although gynecologic, urinary and bowel causes must be excluded.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; StatPearls - Appendicitis

name: Right upper abdominal pain (right upper quadrant)
description: Right upper quadrant pain is pain localized beneath the right costal margin, overlying the liver, gallbladder and biliary tree, with contributions from the duodenum, right kidney, hepatic flexure and right lung base. Biliary pain is often steady and may radiate to the right scapula, whereas hepatic pain from capsular stretch is usually a dull ache accompanying hepatitis or congestion.
weight_rationale: Localization to the right upper quadrant focuses the differential on hepatobiliary disease (cholecystitis, biliary colic, cholangitis, hepatitis), although duodenal, pancreatic, renal and basal pulmonary causes remain possible.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; StatPearls

name: Runny nose (coryza)
description: Rhinorrhea is discharge of fluid from the nose, often with nasal congestion, caused by inflamed nasal mucosa and blood vessels. Coryza (runny nose with sneezing and congestion) is typical of viral upper respiratory infections and is part of the measles prodrome.
weight_rationale: Runny nose points to the upper respiratory tract but is common to colds, influenza, allergy and measles.

name: Seizures (fits or convulsions)
description: Episodes of abnormal electrical activity in the brain causing jerking movements, stiffening, staring or loss of awareness. A first seizure, a seizure with fever in an adult, or one lasting more than 5 minutes needs urgent medical assessment.
weight_rationale: Seizures have many causes; with fever and altered consciousness they raise concern for meningitis or encephalitis and need urgent care.

name: Sensitivity to light (photophobia)
description: Photophobia is discomfort or pain in the eyes in response to bright light. It is a common feature of migraine and also occurs with meningitis, subarachnoid hemorrhage and inflammatory eye disease.
weight_rationale: Photophobia with headache favours migraine but is also a feature of meningeal irritation, giving moderate specificity.

name: Shaky hands (tremor)
description: Rhythmic, involuntary shaking, most often of the hands. A fine, fast tremor seen with arms outstretched is typical of hyperthyroidism, anxiety and stimulants; a slower tremor at rest suggests Parkinson disease.
weight_rationale: A fine tremor of outstretched hands supports hyperthyroidism when combined with other features, but tremor alone is common and nonspecific.

name: Shortness of breath (dyspnea)
description: Dyspnea is a subjective sensation of uncomfortable or difficult breathing, or of not getting enough air. It arises from respiratory, cardiac, metabolic, hematologic and psychological causes, and severe or sudden dyspnea can indicate a life-threatening condition.
weight_rationale: Breathlessness points to cardiopulmonary disease but is shared by many respiratory, cardiac and systemic conditions.

name: Signs of dehydration (sunken eyes, dry mouth, intense thirst)
description: Dehydration is a deficit of body water and electrolytes from fluid losses exceeding intake, most often from diarrhea, vomiting, fever, sweating or osmotic diuresis. Clinical signs progress from thirst, dry mucous membranes and reduced dark urine to sunken eyes, reduced skin turgor, tachycardia, confusion and hypovolemic shock.
weight_rationale: Dehydration reflects severity of fluid loss rather than a specific diagnosis; it narrows attention to diarrheal and vomiting illnesses, uncontrolled hyperglycemia and heat illness, and determines urgency of rehydration.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia; World Health Organization

name: Skin rash
description: A rash is a change in the colour, texture or feel of the skin, which may be macular, papular, vesicular, petechial or urticarial. In febrile illness, a generalized exanthem accompanies many viral infections (e.g., measles, dengue) and some bacterial and drug-related conditions.
weight_rationale: Rash is shared by many infections and drug reactions, but its morphology and distribution add useful discriminating information.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia

name: Slurred or difficult speech
description: Speech difficulty includes dysarthria (slurred, poorly articulated speech from weakness or incoordination of speech muscles) and aphasia (impaired production or comprehension of language from injury to the dominant hemisphere). Sudden onset is a classic warning sign of stroke.
weight_rationale: Sudden slurred speech or language disturbance localises to the brain and strongly suggests stroke or transient ischemic attack.

name: Sore throat
description: Sore throat is discomfort, pain or scratchiness in the throat that often makes swallowing painful. Most cases are due to viral upper respiratory infection; group A streptococcus is the main bacterial cause.
weight_rationale: Sore throat localises disease to the upper respiratory tract but is shared by many viral and bacterial infections.

name: Spoon-shaped, brittle nails (koilonychia)
description: Thin, brittle nails that become flat and then concave, so that the nail can hold a drop of water (spoon nails). It is classically linked to chronic iron deficiency, and can be normal in infants or follow trauma and occupational exposure.
weight_rationale: Koilonychia is uncommon but, when present, strongly suggests long-standing iron deficiency.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; StatPearls - Iron-Deficiency Anemia

name: Stiff neck (neck stiffness)
description: Pain and resistance when bending the chin toward the chest, caused by irritation of the meninges. Together with fever and headache or confusion it is a classic sign of meningitis; Kernig and Brudzinski signs test the same irritation. Muscle strain and neck arthritis also cause stiffness, but usually without fever.
weight_rationale: With fever and headache, a stiff neck strongly suggests meningitis and needs emergency assessment, although its absence does not rule meningitis out.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; StatPearls - Bacterial Meningitis

name: Sudden hot, red, swollen big-toe joint (podagra)
description: Acute inflammation of the joint at the base of the big toe (first metatarsophalangeal joint), with severe pain, swelling, redness and warmth that peak within 24 hours, often starting at night. It is the most typical first presentation of gout; septic arthritis must be considered if there is fever or the person is unwell.
weight_rationale: An acute, exquisitely painful, red and swollen first toe joint reaching peak within a day is the classic presentation of a gout flare.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; StatPearls - Gout

name: Suprapubic pain
description: Suprapubic pain is discomfort in the lower midline abdomen above the pubic bone, over the bladder. It is a typical feature of acute cystitis, and suprapubic tenderness may be found on examination.
weight_rationale: Suprapubic pain with dysuria and frequency points strongly to lower urinary tract infection.

name: Sweating (diaphoresis)
description: Diaphoresis is profuse sweating out of proportion to temperature or activity. It accompanies fever and its defervescence, and cold sweats occur with sympathetic activation in acute coronary syndrome, hypoglycemia, shock and pain.
weight_rationale: Sweating has many physiological and pathological causes, but diaphoresis with chest pain raises concern for myocardial infarction.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia

name: Swelling at the front of the neck (goiter)
description: Enlargement of the thyroid gland, seen or felt as a swelling at the front of the neck that moves up on swallowing. It may be diffuse (Graves disease, iodine deficiency, thyroiditis) or nodular, and thyroid function can be high, normal or low.
weight_rationale: A diffuse, smooth goiter in a person with hyperthyroid symptoms suggests Graves disease; goiter also occurs with iodine deficiency and thyroid nodules.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; StatPearls - Graves Disease

name: Swollen lymph nodes (lymphadenopathy)
description: Lymphadenopathy is enlargement of lymph nodes in size, consistency or number, localized to one region or generalized across two or more non-contiguous regions. Most is reactive to infection, but size, consistency, fixation, location (especially supraclavicular) and duration help separate benign from malignant or systemic causes.
weight_rationale: Enlarged nodes are common and mostly reactive; generalized lymphadenopathy or hard, fixed or supraclavicular nodes narrow the differential toward HIV, tuberculosis, lymphoma and metastatic cancer.
source_attribution: Bates' Guide to Physical Examination and History Taking; MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia; StatPearls

name: Thin wavy lines between fingers or on wrists (burrows)
description: Short, thread-like, grey or skin-colored wavy lines a few millimetres long, made by the scabies mite tunneling in the top layer of skin. They are found mainly in the finger webs, wrists, elbows, belt line, genitals and, in infants, palms and soles, with intense itching that is worse at night.
weight_rationale: Burrows in the finger webs and wrists, with night-time itch in several household members, are almost diagnostic of scabies.

name: Unintentional weight loss
description: Unintentional weight loss is a decrease in body weight that occurs without deliberate dieting or exercise. Clinically significant loss (commonly defined as more than 5% of body weight over 6-12 months) warrants evaluation for malignancy, chronic infection, endocrine and gastrointestinal disease.
weight_rationale: Unintentional weight loss narrows the differential toward chronic infection, malignancy and endocrine disease but remains broad.

name: Urinary frequency & urgency
description: Urinary frequency is the need to urinate more often than usual, and urgency is a sudden, strong need to urinate. Together they are typical of bladder irritation from infection, but also occur with overactive bladder, prostatic enlargement, pregnancy and diabetes.
weight_rationale: Frequency with urgency points to the lower urinary tract, most often cystitis, but overlaps with polyuric states.

name: Visual aura
description: A visual aura is a transient, fully reversible visual disturbance that develops gradually over at least 5 minutes and lasts up to 60 minutes, often preceding migraine headache. It typically begins as a small area of vision loss or bright shimmering lines (scintillating scotoma) that expands across the visual field.
weight_rationale: A gradually spreading, positive visual disturbance lasting 5-60 minutes is highly characteristic of migraine with aura.

name: Vomiting after coughing fits (post-tussive vomiting)
description: Post-tussive vomiting is vomiting provoked by a severe bout of coughing, caused by the rise in intrathoracic and intra-abdominal pressure and vagal stimulation during paroxysms. It is a characteristic feature of pertussis and should prompt consideration of that diagnosis whenever vomiting follows coughing.
weight_rationale: Vomiting triggered by coughing paroxysms is a recognized clinical criterion for pertussis and considerably raises its likelihood, although forceful coughing from other causes can occasionally do the same.

name: Vomiting blood (hematemesis)
description: Hematemesis is vomiting of fresh blood, clots or dark 'coffee-ground' material from the upper gastrointestinal tract. It indicates bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz and requires assessment for hemodynamic instability.
weight_rationale: Vomiting blood localises bleeding to the upper gastrointestinal tract and is a strong pointer toward peptic ulcer, varices or mucosal tears.

name: Waking at night to urinate (nocturia)
description: Waking from sleep one or more times to pass urine. Causes include high evening fluid or caffeine intake, bladder and prostate problems, diabetes (high urine volume), heart failure (fluid shifted at night) and chronic kidney disease, in which the kidneys lose the ability to concentrate urine.
weight_rationale: Nocturia is common and nonspecific; in chronic kidney disease it reflects loss of urine-concentrating ability, but it is more often due to fluid intake, prostate disease or diabetes.

name: Wheezing
description: Wheezing is a high-pitched, musical sound produced by airflow through narrowed or compressed airways, usually most prominent on expiration. It is characteristic of asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, but 'all that wheezes is not asthma'.
weight_rationale: Wheeze indicates airway narrowing and strongly favours obstructive airway diseases such as asthma and COPD.

name: White patches in the mouth (oral thrush)
description: Oral thrush is Candida overgrowth in the mouth, classically forming creamy white, curd-like plaques on the tongue, buccal mucosa and palate that can be wiped off to leave a red, sometimes bleeding surface. Outside infancy, denture use, antibiotics and inhaled or systemic corticosteroids, it suggests impaired cell-mediated immunity and is an important clinical marker of HIV infection.
weight_rationale: Wipeable white plaques are highly characteristic of candidiasis, and unexplained thrush in an adult strongly suggests immunosuppression, notably HIV, or uncontrolled diabetes.
